chapters.title: Chapter 6: Tax, the Buy Decision and Your Portfolio

lessons.title: Buy vs Rent: Running the Numbers on a Bengaluru Flat

children.text: Karthik and Divya, both 31, work in tech in Whitefield, Bengaluru and pay ₹40,000 a month to rent a 2BHK. At every family function someone tells them the same thing: "Rent is dead money. Buy a flat." A similar flat in their society costs ₹1.2 crore. Should they buy? Instead of arguing, this lesson runs the actual numbers over 10 years, compares the buyer's wealth with a renter who invests the difference, and shows you exactly what the answer depends on.

body.text: "Rent is dead money" ignores that interest, stamp duty and maintenance are dead money too. The real question is who ends up wealthier: the buyer, or a disciplined renter who invests every rupee the buyer would have spent extra.

cells: ₹24 lakh down payment + about ₹10 lakh stamp duty, registration and other costs = ₹34 lakh
₹34 lakh invested in a Nifty 50 index fund on day one
EMI on ₹96 lakh at 8% for 20 years, plus maintenance and property tax
Nothing: it is spent on the home
Invested every month in the same index fund
Maintenance ₹4,000 a month and property tax ₹15,000 a year, both rising 5% a year
Sell the flat, pay 1% brokerage plus GST, repay the loan
Redeem the fund and pay long-term capital gains tax

children.text: To keep the comparison clean, the model assumes the new tax regime, where self-occupied home loan interest is not deductible, and ignores capital gains tax on the flat, as if the proceeds were reinvested in another home. Both simplifications slightly favour buying.

body.title: What the renter gets to invest
body.prompt: In year 1, the buyer's monthly outflow is ₹85,548 and the renter pays ₹40,000 in rent. If the renter invests the entire difference, how much goes into the index fund each month, in ₹?
body.explanation: ₹85,548 minus ₹40,000 = ₹45,548 a month. As rent rises 5% a year and the EMI stays flat, this gap narrows over time, but in the early years it is a large monthly investment.

body.label: Dead money, year 1
body.value: Buyer: about ₹7.6 lakh in interest plus ₹10 lakh in stamp duty and costs. Renter: ₹4.8 lakh in rent.
body.context: About ₹64,000 of the buyer's very first ₹80,298 EMI is interest. Principal repayment builds ownership, but interest, stamp duty, maintenance and property tax are gone as surely as rent.

body.caption: The renter's wealth is the value of the index fund after long-term capital gains tax.

body.title: Buyer vs renter wealth after 10 years, with a 10% fund return (₹ lakh)
Show me how the numbers were built

children.text: Loan: ₹96 lakh at 8% for 20 years gives an EMI of ₹80,298. After 10 years, about ₹66.2 lakh is still outstanding.
Buyer's wealth at 5% growth: ₹1.2 crore × 1.05^10 = ₹1.955 crore; less 1.18% brokerage with GST; less ₹66.2 lakh loan = about ₹1.27 crore.
Renter: invests ₹34 lakh on day one plus the monthly gap between the buyer's costs and rent, calculated month by month. Total contributions over 10 years are about ₹77.9 lakh.
Renter's tax: long-term capital gains above ₹1.25 lakh taxed at 12.5% at redemption.
Not modelled: home loan tax benefits under the old regime, capital gains tax on the flat, rental security deposits, moving costs, and major repairs. Change any of these and the answer shifts.

The single most useful output of this model is the break-even appreciation: how fast the flat's price must grow each year for buying to match renting and investing. It depends on what the renter's investments earn.

body.caption: Annual price growth needed for buying to match renting (10 years, illustrative)

body.text: Put the break-even in context. ANAROCK data shows Bengaluru prices up about 90% from 2019 to mid-2026, roughly 9.6% a year, during a strong upcycle. RBI's All-India House Price Index, by contrast, grew only 2.2% to 4.2% a year across 2025-26. If you believe Whitefield prices will keep compounding above about 6.4% a year for a decade, buying wins. If not, renting and investing likely leaves you wealthier.

children.text: A Quick Rule of Thumb: The Price-to-Rent Ratio

body.caption: Karthik and Divya's flat: ₹1.2 crore ÷ ₹4.8 lakh = 25.
Reading the price-to-rent ratio (a rough guide, not a rule)

cells: Rent is expensive relative to price; buying tends to look attractive
A grey zone where assumptions decide the answer
Prices are high relative to rent; renting and investing often wins unless strong appreciation follows

body.title: Calculate the ratio
body.prompt: A 3BHK in Koramangala costs ₹2.4 crore and rents for ₹65,000 a month. What is its price-to-rent ratio? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Annual rent: ₹65,000 × 12 = ₹7.8 lakh. Ratio: ₹2.4 crore ÷ ₹7.8 lakh = 30.8. That is high: the flat costs almost 31 years of rent, so buying it as a pure financial decision needs strong price growth to beat renting.

body.title: Complete the formula
body.textWithBlank: The price-to-rent ratio is the property's price divided by its annual ___.
body.explanation: Price ÷ annual rent. It is the inverse of gross rental yield: a ratio of 25 means a gross yield of 4%.

columns.label: Good reasons to buy
points: Stability: no landlord can ask you to leave or raise rent sharply
Freedom to renovate and make the home your own
Forced savings through EMIs, if you would not invest the difference otherwise
A rent-free home in retirement once the loan is repaid
Settled plans: long-term job, schools and family in the same city

columns.label: Good reasons to rent
points: Flexibility to move for a better job or a different city
No large down payment, stamp duty or major repair bills
Wealth stays liquid and diversified instead of locked in one flat
Lower financial stress if income is uncertain
The ability to live in a better area than you could afford to buy in

body.text: The renter only wins if the difference is actually invested, every month, for a decade, through market crashes. Many renters spend it on a bigger car, holidays or upgrades instead. If you know you will not invest the gap, the forced savings of an EMI may genuinely leave you better off, even when the spreadsheet says otherwise.

body.title: What tips the balance?
body.question: Which change would make buying a flat more attractive compared with renting and investing?
options: Home loan rates rise from 8% to 9.5%
Rents in the area rise sharply while flat prices stay the same
Equity market returns are expected to be higher
The buyer expects to move cities in three years
body.explanation: Higher rents with unchanged prices lower the price-to-rent ratio: renting becomes costlier and the renter has less to invest. Higher loan rates, better equity returns and a likely move all favour renting.

body.title: Karthik and Divya decide
body.scenario: Karthik and Divya have ₹36 lakh saved. Divya may get an offer to move to her company's Pune office within two to three years. Karthik is confident Whitefield prices will keep rising 8% a year. They both invest regularly through SIPs and have never missed one.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, what should they consider before deciding?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The likely move matters most: a move in two or three years means paying stamp duty and buying costs of about ₹10 lakh, then selling costs, within a short period. Round-trip costs alone could wipe out several years of appreciation. That strongly favours renting for now.
2. Test Karthik's 8% belief: it is above the model's break-even of about 6.4% at a 10% fund return, but it is a forecast. They should also model 3% to 5%, where renting wins clearly.
3. Price-to-rent of 25: the flat is priced high relative to rent, which leans towards renting unless appreciation stays strong.
4. Their discipline is a strength: since they reliably invest through SIPs, they are exactly the kind of renters who capture the model's advantage.
5. Liquidity and safety: buying would consume ₹34 lakh of their ₹36 lakh, leaving almost no emergency fund.
6. A reasonable conclusion: keep renting while the Pune move is uncertain, keep investing the difference, and revisit the decision once their city and jobs are settled for the long term.

body.title: Run Your Own Buy vs Rent Decision
steps: Find the price and current rent of the same kind of flat in the same society
Add every buying cost: down payment, stamp duty, registration, interiors
Compare the buyer's monthly outflow (EMI, maintenance, property tax) with rent
Estimate how many years you will realistically stay in this city
Model several price growth rates and fund returns, not just the optimistic case
Be honest about whether you would invest the monthly difference
Keep an emergency fund in either path

cards.definition: Money spent that builds no wealth: rent for renters; interest, stamp duty, maintenance and property tax for buyers.
Renting while investing the extra money a buyer would spend, then comparing wealth after a set period.
The annual price growth at which buying and renting-and-investing leave you equally wealthy.
Flat price divided by annual rent. Higher ratios tend to favour renting.
The way EMIs compel regular principal repayment, useful for people who would not otherwise save.
Buying and selling costs combined, which punish owners who move within a few years.

points: "Rent is dead money" ignores that interest, stamp duty, maintenance and property tax are also dead money.
In our Whitefield model, the buyer spent ₹85,548 a month in year 1 versus ₹40,000 rent, and the renter invested the ₹45,548 gap.
After 10 years, buying won only when flat prices grew faster than about 6.4% a year, assuming a 10% fund return.
A price-to-rent ratio above about 25 generally tilts the decision towards renting unless strong appreciation follows.
A likely move within a few years strongly favours renting because of heavy buying and selling costs.
The numbers matter, but so do stability, flexibility and whether you will truly invest the difference.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not financial, tax or investment advice. The buy vs rent model uses simplified, illustrative assumptions; actual prices, rents, loan rates, tax treatment and investment returns will differ. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a tax professional before making housing or investment decisions.
